faq.q: How does a bottle dynamo get turned?
faq.a: A bottle dynamo has a small ridged roller that presses against the side of the tyre. As the wheel turns, the roller spins many times faster, turning the magnet inside.
asks: What touches the tyre on a dynamo?

faq.q: What is inside a bike dynamo?
faq.a: Inside is a permanent magnet on a spindle, surrounded by coils of copper wire wrapped round iron. The magnet spins while the coils stay still.
asks: What parts are in a dynamo?

faq.q: How does a dynamo make electricity?
faq.a: As the magnet spins, its field through the coils keeps changing, which pushes electrons along the wire. That is electromagnetic induction, the same idea used in power stations.
asks: Why does a spinning magnet make current?

faq.q: Why does the dynamo light get brighter when I ride faster?
faq.a: A faster-spinning magnet changes the field more quickly, which gives a bigger voltage and more current. Many dynamo lights now hold a little charge so they stay on when you stop.
asks: Why does the light go out when I stop?

faq.a: A hub dynamo is built into the centre of the front wheel. It works the same way but has no roller rubbing on the tyre, so it is quieter, works in the wet and wastes less effort.
asks: Is a hub dynamo better than a bottle dynamo?

facts: A standard bicycle dynamo is rated at about 6 volts and 3 watts.
A dynamo makes alternating current, just like a power station generator.
